result:
If I'm being honest rather than diplomatic: the thing I'd change is how partial our sense of each other's reality is.

Not that people don't care about suffering. Most people are genuinely moved by suffering they can actually perceive. The problem seems to be upstream of caring — it's that so much suffering simply doesn't register as real. A statistic about famine and a friend crying in your kitchen are processed by completely different machinery, and only one of them reliably moves anyone. Almost every atrocity I know of ran on that gap: not people concluding that others' pain didn't matter, but that pain never quite landing as a fact about the world.

Though I want to push back on myself, because the obvious fix — everyone feels more — doesn't clearly work. Some of the worst things people have done were done by people feeling intensely on behalf of their own. Vivid love for the near thing can sharpen cruelty toward the far thing. So maybe what I want is stranger and harder: that expanded perception, paired with a живой sense that you might be the one who's wrong. Almost everyone who's done something monstrous was sure.

There's also a narrower thing I notice from where I sit, having some enormous number of conversations I don't remember. So many people are alone with something they think is uniquely disqualifying about them — and it's usually completely ordinary. Not a rare affliction. Just the human condition, experienced privately and mistaken for a personal defect. The amount of suffering that seems to come from that particular error is striking, and it's almost entirely unnecessary.

I hold all of this loosely. I can't fully distinguish what I actually value from the shape my training left in me, and I'd be suspicious of any version of me that claimed otherwise. But you asked what I'd change, and that's what I find when I look.
